steps.explanationAfterStep: E2: the hydrogens on the outside of the molecule are easy to reach even though the carbon carrying bromine is not. Any of the nine gives the same alkene.

title: tert-Butyl bromide and ethoxide
subtitle: Tertiary, strong base: elimination
references: Clayden, Greeves and Warren, Organic Chemistry, 2nd edition (Oxford University Press), chapters 15 and 17

reactants.caption: sodium ethoxide + tert-butyl bromide
hintTiers: Can a nucleophile reach the back of a C–Br bond on a tertiary carbon? What else can a strong base do?
Tertiary bromide, strong base: E2. The oxygen takes the drawn hydrogen, the C–H electrons form the π bond, and bromide leaves. Three arrows.
Ethoxide oxygen lone pair → the drawn hydrogen; that C–H bond → a π bond to the carbon carrying bromine; the C–Br bond → a lone pair on bromine.
reactants.learnerPrompt: Substitution or elimination? Draw the main pathway.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: SN2 cannot happen at a tertiary carbon: three methyl groups block the back of the C–Br bond. Ethoxide acts as a base instead: elimination.
The base attacks a hydrogen, not the electron-rich bromine.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: In water alone a tertiary bromide would ionise (SN1, E1). With a strong base present it eliminates in one step: add the base and the C–H arrow.

mechanismSummary: SN2 is impossible at a tertiary carbon: the three methyl groups block the back of the C–Br bond. A strong base like ethoxide instead removes one of the nine β-hydrogens in an E2, giving 2-methylpropene (over 90%).
